Thanks for the review @kevinmcconnell!

Yeah finding the right names and APIs for this has been unexpectedly hard. I've gone from the entries being associated to the bubble, to now having an explicit AR `thread` model (which seems odd but gives us an idiomatic cache expiry mechanism and more natural language).

I think the general architecture here is a good direction, just gotta find the right names and framing to make it roll off the tongue and feel natural.

I might switch gears today and let ideas gestate. I'd like to try and ship the un-nesting of bucket views today, too, and come back with a fresh mind.

> an explicit AR thread model (which seems odd but gives us an idiomatic cache expiry mechanism and more natural language)

Re the caching of the `Thread` model, do you mean you wanted an additional level of fragment caching between the `Bubble` and it's `Threadable`s? I'm curious whether that would matter in practice, since a lot of `Bubble` changes will presumably also be adding events. I'd guess it's more important that each `Threadable` gets cached. But in any case, we could separate that fragment out without giving it its own model if it's worthwhile?

In terms of language, I think "a bubble has many comments" feels more natural than "a bubble has one thread, which has many comments". But maybe I'm missing something here! Did you find some parts come out more awkwardly without that model?

> I'm curious whether that would matter in practice, since a lot of Bubble changes will presumably also be adding events. I'd guess it's more important that each Threadable gets cached. But in any case, we could separate that fragment out without giving it its own model if it's worthwhile?

I suspect you're right! That's why I didn't start out with the thread, but then I might've been influenced by calling these "thread entries" from the start, to your point about a bubble having a thread, which has many comments (or thread entries, currently).

Yes, the naming might be the only thing suggesting it! "Thread entry" is a tricky name because of that, it implies there is a "Thread" they belong to, whereas having a collection of "Comments" didn't imply any sort of "Comment list". But aside from the names, the relationships are equivalent. I reckon the "thread entry" name is just a little misleading.

I almost wondered if the `Entry`/`Entryable` naming, like in HEY, could work here. It doesn't feel quite right to say "a bubble has many entries", but it's close. On the other hand, we're showing two types of message on the bubble: user messages (comments) and system messages (event summaries), which is what led me to think of this as `Message`/`Messageable`. Something along these lines could make sense.

One thing about having a materialized `thread` is that we can also later have a concept of a global `timeline`, and we can choose to relay events to the `thread` and/or `timeline` as needed. That's what the rollup kind of is — a relay mechanism. But that's getting too far ahead of ourselves.

Let's go with the simplest architecture for now (likely your proposed `Message/Messageable` directly on the bubble, which doesn't impede relaying to a timeline either) and accept that this is in flux so we can keep iterating on everything. I'm not sure we know enough about the product yet to make a definitive decision here. As long as it's easy to change, cache, and paginate (which we do know we want) we can move forward.

Made the change to having messages directly on the bubble and I'm quite happy with it. I don't think we'll miss the `thread`, but we'll see where the product takes us.

I think this is at a point where we can stop tinkering with it. Gonna give the PR a once-over for cleanup and merge. Happy to take any retroactive feedback though!

EDIT: Ope, got pretty timely feedback — I'll just address that before merging.

Thanks for the review @kevinmcconnell!

> What do you think?

Responded as part of this thread: https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/pull/129#discussion_r1828165373

Will think some more about this today

I like the direction this is going. Not having saved filters for the bucket views is what I was getting at yesterday, and I think the `Filter` name works quite well in practice rather than `View` :+1: 

I'm still a little unsure of some of the details of the modelling though. Maybe it's just me. But `Bucket` seems to have two different responsibilities now: it's the primary method of organizing bubbles and granting access to them (i.e. `Bubble belongs_to :bucket`), which is what it was before; but it's also now the mechanism we use to show groupings of bubbles on the index. Some of the bucket relationships seem a little inconsistent as a result. For example, a user's accessible bubbles is defined by buckets, but only certain types of buckets (the ones with `Project` bucketables). And a `Filter` may want to show bubbles from certain projects, but it's doing that by way of `Bucket` (but again, only the `Project`-related buckets).b Do you know what I mean? Or are you thinking of this differently?

I wonder if `Bubbles` should actually belong to `Projects`. And in a filter, if you choose a specific project to filter on, you'd be adding a condition on that `Project` rather than its `Bubble`. In other words, a `Project` would be the grouping criteria that bubbles fit into, and a `Bucket` is the abstract way of preventing a collection of bubbles in the UI (which, using the delegated types, can be to show a specific `Project`, or a user-defined `Filter`).

Unrelated, but in terms of the sorting, how will that work with user-defined filters? If a bubble touches its bucket, does this mean that bucket filters will rise to the top when their contents change, but user-defined filters will rise to the top if they are edited?

Per our call today, I'm gonna park the work here and close the PR for future reference. It seems it's too early to make architecture decisions around filters.

Specifically, we're not sure we'll want to list filters and projects together. It's possible we might want to list them separately. Which means we can opt for a simpler model and simpler code.

However, we do know we want to unnest bubbles, save query params as filters, and query for multiple values per field, all of which was part of this PR. I'll cherry-pick those parts in a new PR so we can keep this as reference in case we decide we do want this type of architecture down the line.

It's quite powerful and does everything we want it to. But it's more complicated than simply storing the query params for later. Then again, we _are_ doing some clever things so there's bound to be reasonable complexity. Let me know what you think!

I spiked out the plain ol' form approach, but I bailed when I realized we'd need a ton of JS to replicate what Hotwire gives us for free if we're willing to hit the server. EDIT: Gah, realized after writing my original comment that there might be simpler approaches than my spike from today. And in replacing the complexity from the current approach it might be a wash in the end. Retracting my original comment for now so I can reconsider with a fresh mind tomorrow. Here's the original comment for reference:
Original comment In the regular form approach we'd be:
  • Pre-rendering all chips for all possible filters (which can mean quite a lot as the account grows and more assigner/assignee and bucket filters become available — not prohibitively many but worth mentioning)
  • Juggling state as we mimic radio-button and checkbox selection with the chips
    • This is exacerbated by having to mimic based on filter kind e.g. clicking a radio button only removes chips of a certain kind — although this is also a thing in the current implementation
  • Writing JS logic to wire up how each filter should be mimicked
    • Clicking on a radio button removes chips of the same kind
    • Clicking on a checkbox accumulates chips of the same kind
    • Clicking certain buttons clears all chips of a kind (all projects)
    • Clicking other buttons adds a chip in addition to clearing other chips (unassigned)
The chips are also rendered semi-far in terms of markup from the buttons. Which probably means finding the proper chip to activate based on `aria-controls`. It just gets messy pretty quick. Finally, the regular form approach locks us out of adding search terms to filters since those can't be pre-rendered. Although we did mention in the call this wasn't a hard requirement and were happy to cut that out of scope. But! The ~~Hotwire~~ Turbo Streams approach permits search terms — for what it's worth. I got far enough to know it's possible. And I realize the current approach isn't free of complexity. But I think we should lean hard on Hotwire for this one. Let me know if you have strong feelings otherwise.
On another note, @jzimdars I think I managed to mitigate all the disorienting flickering by creating "zones" (via turbo frames) for each kind of filter. It's rather nice, because all filters of the same kind are always grouped together. And we consistently display the filters in the same order every time.

> Pre-rendering all chips for all possible filters (which can mean quite a lot as the account grows and more

I think this will be fine. It's really just a list of buttons, so it won't be a ton of markup. And I think converting the multiple form approach to a single form will reduce the markup overall (due to rendering less per filter option), so this way could well come out ahead.

> Writing JS logic to wire up how each filter should be mimicked ... Clicking on a radio button removes chips of the same kind ...

The idea behind the single form is that you _don't_ need to do this, because radio buttons already work this way. Same for checkboxes. We'd need some JS for the cases that HTML can't provide natively (like adding a button that clears a set of radio buttons), but if we layer that on top of the built-in behavior it may not be a lot. I think question will come down to what that extra layering needs to look like.

> Juggling state as we mimic radio-button and checkbox selection with the chips

The thinking here was that every checkbox/radio button on the form has a corresponding chip. If the input is checked, the chip is visible. And if you click the chip, the input resets. So there's not really any state to juggle other than connecting those pairs. (Maybe there are edge cases for the default options, but we might be able to extend the same pattern for those too.)

> The chips are also rendered semi-far in terms of markup from the buttons. Which probably means finding the proper chip to activate based on aria-controls. It just gets messy pretty quick.

They'll all be inside the same container (perhaps the `form`) so it shouldn't be too bad. We could connect their IDs with data attributes.

> the regular form approach locks us out of adding search terms to filters since those can't be pre-rendered.

That's the biggest issue, I think. If we want to keep the ability to add multiple search sections, then perhaps that one part of the form still needs to be dynamic. Possibly it comes out simpler to have only a specific dynamic part (given that section of the form already works a little differently than the other options), but we'd have to see.

Anyway, I don't think we need to spend too long going down this rabbit hole if it doesn't feel promising. It's worth looking it to see where it leads, but if it continues to look like a dead end you'll be the best judge of when to abandon it.

> and see how hard we can lean on Hotwire for things like this

Also agree on this point -- as a general principle it's a very good thing to keep in mind :+1: 

> That, and accessibility, might dictate what we go with in the end.

Yeah, I've been wondering about the accessibility side of this too. In the single form design that seems easy to understand: the form inputs would have the expected semantic meaning in terms of what is or isn't selected in the filter and what can be changed on it, so I would guess we'd be pretty close by default.

With the multiple form approach, I'm not quite as sure, but I wonder if the way to think about it is that, conceptually, this is a section describing the current filter and the options to de-select each clause (the bar of chips along the top), followed by a number of sections of "Add {something} to the filter" choices. If that way works from an accessibility point of view, it may also be straightforward. I'm just guessing though. Could be worth looping in @brunoprietog to get his thoughts on this, particularly if there are any complications or downsides that we might not have thought of?

FWIW, I'd imagined this as a single form in the sense that you'd make all of your selections and then "apply" the filter rather than it updating the view after every new choice. Some shopping websites do that latter and it always feels/is slow. One thing we could try if it were to simplify things is to not show the chips while the form is open. Then there wouldn't be anything to update live on the page. Something like this:

Thanks! 😄

> rather than it updating the view after every new choice.

We currently update the view in the sense that we add a chip, but the filters aren't applied until you click "apply". That said, trying this out in production is slower than I thought it'd be — the chip sometimes takes too long to appear.

Removing the chips and search field does greatly simplify things, and better adheres to web standards. In fact, it should be incredibly simple to spike. I'd expect minimal JS. I'll do that today, I think we're going to like the result.

A shame to lose the search terms, but that was never a hard requirement anyway.

This is looking good. I'd say the best way to route around the issue with the prototenant is simply to ensure you're not accessing any tenanted models until the tenant has been created. So instead of doing `form_with model: User.new`, I'd just do `form_with url: ...` and then manually scope the attributes in the form. Then you're free from having to lean on attribute metadata introspection before you're within the tenant scope.

@kevinmcconnell Thanks for the thoughtful comments. Lots to unpack, but in brief:

1. I wasn't aware that we are thinking about upstreaming some form of the markdown model into Rails, that's helpful to know! 👍
2. Your comments have validated my uneasiness with the models' design. 😬
3. I agree that we probably need to rethink some aspects of how this is designed, in particular where the `slug` lives. (More on this below.)

## the Attachment model

> ... content was pasted from one bubble to another ... should be allowed, and it's probably useful to do it sometimes. And even if it hasn't happened yet, presumably it could in the future?

Yup, I ran and tested the migration script on production data, and that revealed a handful of slugs that appear in 2 comments each, though it just so happens that the pairs of comments in question both belong to the same Bubble.

It's obviously also possible for an attachment to appear in multiple bubbles (and multiple collections) if someone copy-pastes the uploads link into a new bubble. That's notable because doing so would create an _implicit_ "attachment" that's not reflected in the database as an `Attachment`, with implications for garbage collection of blobs and incorrect results from features like "view attachments for this collection".

If I was modeling this from scratch:

1. I agree the `Attachment` should either be on the `ActionText::Markdown` or, as you suggest, the record that `has_markdown`.
2. When the `slug` of an existing `Attachment` is pasted into a new `Comment`, we should really detect that and create a new `Attachment`.
   Which forces me to unfortunately conclude ...
3. `slug` should not be on the `Attachment` model, it should really be on the `Blob`. 😮‍💨

And if we put the `slug` on the `Blob` model, that implies the `UploadsController` manages a truly global resource (`BlobsController`?) that is cleanly separated from the act of attaching that upload/blob to a comment (which simplifies all the form actions, I think).


## the Markdown model

If I'm being totally honest, this all feels harder than it should be at the moment because the Markdown model doesn't have any affordances for finding or replacing `slug`s, we're really relying on markdown links "just working" when they're pasted.

So at the risk of expanding the scope here, perhaps we want to explore ways to turn the markdown into more structured data (like an AST) in order to more reliably find URLs and compare them against known/existing slugs.


## next steps

I'm going to take another swing at this,

- moving the attachment association to the Comment model, and
- moving the slug to be an attribute (via association) of Blob (not Attachment)

and see how it feels. If it's going OK, then I'm going to explore introducing a methods like `#links` that will return the hyperlinks from the markdown content, and see if that's useful to make it easier to detect a new reference to an existing Blob.

WDYT?

@jorgemanrubia I think the approach makes sense, but I also had a different idea in mind and wondered what you think of this as an alternative. The way I see it, mentions are not themselves notifiable things, because they always happen in the context of some other event that _is_ notifiable: a new comment, a new card, etc. So I think the mentions state is more a property of the resource, and instead of adding new notifications we just need to make the current notification content reflect that.

For example, if I create a comment that mentions you, I don't think you need to receive both of these:

- "Kevin commented on {card}"
- "Kevin mentioned you on {card}"

I think the second implies the first, and can be thought of as just the "commented" notification being a bit more detailed. (cc @jzimdars -- does this sound right to you?).

We do something similar(ish) already with assignments: we don't send you a "Kevin created {card}" if we're already sending you "Kevin assigned you to {card}".

So what I had in mind is that we could keep notifications on events, because everything that's notifiable is a trackable event, by design. And instead the flow works something like this:

- When a comment is saved, we update its associated mentions
- New mentions also add new watches (so that mentionees become watchers automatially)
- When notifying of a comment or creation, say whether you were mentioned or not (via a `notification.resource.mentions?(user)` or something like that)

The current notifications system should already take care of the right audience for these, according to the watching status and each user's notification preferences.

I think this way should be a simpler change, and keeps the notifications & mentions machinery more separate from each other. And means we don't have to think about how to suppress those overlapping notifications (assuming that's the behavior we want; again JZ can probably confirm.)

What do you think?

I think there's something a bit muddy about Notifier and Notifications interact as well. But can't quite put my finger on it yet. Maybe it'll be clear once we've removed some of the other abstraction.

I think a better way to handle overlapping notifications is to skip them when they don't make sense. E.g: we can "published" or "commented" doesn't make sense if the object carries a mention. And we could do the same with assignments, to remove teh "initial assignment" workaround. I'll play with this idea, which should also play well with David's suggestion of simplifying the fine-grained event notifiers.

@jorgemanrubia sure, it's up to you. To me, having only events be notifiable feels simpler conceptually, and I think making different notification sources aware of each other to filter out duplication is adding in some implicit knowledge that makes it a bit more confusing. There was something quite nice about the event trail being the central stream that ties notifications back into the events that we show in the UI. But I can definitely see both ways.

To use the script:

```
./script/load-prod-db-in-dev.rb path/to/main.sqlite3
```

It will:
- create a new signal identity, queenbee account, signal account, and signal user
- copy the database as the new tenant with the qb account id
- link the Account.sole to the signal account
- link the first user in the database to the signal user and identity
- print out how to login as the user

Output will end with a line like:

```
Login to http://launchpad.localhost:3011/ as dev-cb5e01f9@example.com / secret123456
```

@kevinmcconnell @flavorjones I'd appreciate your eyes on the approach

> I considered using regular Rails caching, but it seemed too weak. The summaries we generate are meaningful pieces of information. I think it makes sense to make them a first-class citizen.

I agree, I think this is spot on 👍

There's another reason I wanted to mention for doing it this way too: with our replicated SQLite setup, each app server will have its own cache (because we can't share those databases across servers, and we want the cache operations to be local and fast). This means that cache content will get duplicated, which in most cases should be fine (it's just a few more cache misses), but in this case we wouldn't want to have to regenerate the content on each server. But storing the content in the model solves this, because it will replicated along with the rest of the app data.

One question I have -- and I think this is currently in-flux anyway with the discussion of linking accounts with different email addresses -- is whether we can/should move the creation of the new tenant to _after_ the magic link step.

I think that would help because:
- We get email address validation before creating a new database. While that's not perfect, it goes a long way to avoid malicious or accidental requests flooding us with a bunch of new tenant DBs. It means you at least need to go through that dance once before you can create a database; and once you're authenticated we could also limit how many/quickly you could create any subsequent ones.
- I think we could then have "Create account" be an option on the same magic link landing page. We could style it differently depending on whether you had existing accounts (but still might want to add another one), or this was your first.
- If you create a new one we can link it then bounce you to the tenanted path to create and populate the DB (possibly moving the actual creation into a job while the front end waits for it to complete, as we discussed).
- All of this would be linked by a single email address still.

I think that's a bit different from what we have here, but how does it compare to where you're heading?

Nice, it would be great if we can validate this idea. Would the plan be to move this to a Rails database resolver middleware rather than a concern after testing?

> Would the plan be to move this to a Rails database resolver middleware rather than a concern after testing?

Yes, I think a middleware makes most sense. The concern is just an easy place to test things out first.

More generally, the part I was wondering about is whether we should lean on the proxy layer to help with this. If we don't, it's nice that this could be self-contained: we could allow configuring the poll interval and max delay, but otherwise all you'd need to do is enable the middleware and it works. But the downside would be if we had a sustained period of high replica lag, suddenly all the requests that follow a recent write become slower, which could affect capacity. Maybe that's fine though, it's an unusual case and there is an upper limit on how bad it can get.

I think it'll be hard to tell without a bit of real-world testing.

If we didn't mind involving custom proxy features, I think there could be a version of this where a stale read condition is returned to the proxy, and it could treat that like the writer pinning situation. So, instead of pinning to the writer for 1s after a write, you optimistically send all reads to the secondary site. But if one of those reads returns a special "stale read" header, you treat it like a pinned write: send it to the writer if it was within 1s of an actual write. That way it could degrade to the previous behaviour when necessary without adding delays at the Puma level. But now it's dependent on specific proxy support, which would be fine for Fizzy but becomes harder to make more generally available.

I'm inclined to try running Fizzy on this simple version for a bit, and gather some data about how it behaves. What do you think?

Two changes will make this config clearer and more reliable across providers:

1. Rename `aws` to `s3`
   The current name implies vendor-specific behavior, but this config works with any S3-compatible service (R2, MinIO, Tigris, DO Spaces). Using `s3` reflects the protocol, not the vendor.

2. Add checksum configuration for non-AWS providers
   [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/#checksum-types) and some MinIO setups reject the default `CRC64NVME` checksum and return `InvalidRequest: You can only specify one non-default checksum at a time`.

   Suggested config:

   ```ruby
   s3:
     service: S3
     # ...existing config...
     request_checksum_calculation: <%= ENV.fetch("S3_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION", "when_supported") %>
     response_checksum_validation: <%= ENV.fetch("S3_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION", "when_supported") %>
    ```

    For R2/MinIO users:
    ```bash
    S3_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required
    S3_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION=when_required
    ```

This keeps AWS behavior unchanged while ensuring compatibility with other S3 providers.

Maybe allow for 1 env-var `SMTP_URL` instead of 8?  
Shameless self-promotion: I created [uri-smtp](https://github.com/eval/uri-smtp?tab=readme-ov-file#urismtp--) that extends URI to understand uri's using smtp(s) protocols:

```diff
+  config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = URI(ENV.fetch("SMTP_URL")).to_h(format: :am)

-  config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = {
-    address: ENV.fetch("SMTP_ADDRESS", "localhost"),
-    port: ENV.fetch("SMTP_PORT", "587").to_i,
-    domain: ENV.fetch("SMTP_DOMAIN", nil),
-    user_name: ENV.fetch("SMTP_USERNAME", nil),
-    password: ENV.fetch("SMTP_PASSWORD", nil),
-    authentication: ENV.fetch("SMTP_AUTHENTICATION", "plain"),
-    enable_starttls_auto: ENV.fetch("SMTP_ENABLE_STARTTLS_AUTO", "true") == "true"
-  }
```

The `SMTP_URL` can now double as `MAILER_DELIVERY_METHOD` - when it's there, use SMTP otherwise use a fallback.

Besides being more convenient to have 1 var, it also:
* ...has proper defaults. 
  e.g. `starttls: :always`, but not for local development (against e.g. mailcatcher), ports for `smtps://..` vs `smtp://...` etc.
* ...works around a bug in mail-gem v2.8.1 that when setting `tls: false`, `starttls` will be ignored
  Probably the reason the rails sample config doesn't contain the tls-setting(?)
* ...provides a consistent config 
  e.g. `tls: true` ánd `starttls: true` (which makes no sense): `URI("smtps://user:pass@gmail.com?starttls=true").starttls #=> false`. `URI("smtp://gmail.com?authentication=plain").auth #=> nil` (prevents net-smtp from raising because there's no authinfo).  
  But to start: weird configurations in URI-form are more easily spotted because they look weird.

@flavorjones Thank you for reviewing. Yes there was a cascade with the three files, that meant I couldn't propose the improvement without the fix. The most impactful was the `deactivate` method in `user.rb`, which is used by both the identity destroy path and the user destroy path. Also with `User.deactivate` @dhh highlighted (7124835) that lengthy transactions (in that method) could cause db lockup issues. 

The answer was to remove the `identity: nil` statement  to satisfy both pathways, but first we had to ensure the callback ordering was correct in identity, otherwise the identity destroy path caused problems, as the commit record attests. 
This also allowed the `transaction` to be removed again (it had been added back) as per dhh's instructions.  Doing all this meant that a user now just has its `active?` flag changed to false and accesses removed. So it made sense to add the enhancement to re-activate the user for the account in `Joinable:join.rb`. Trying to create a new user, when there is already a user with both account_id and identity_id available to reconnect to. Also somebody would expect when rejoining an account to regain access to all their existing comments and cards etc. It all just made sense as a congruent feature as both a fix and an improvement. 

The current situation is that we have merged the `identity destroy` callback ordering fix in #2017 
We have left in this PR to remove `identity: nil` in `User.deactivate` as the identity destroy path already does this and make the user destroy path more efficient and have expected behaviour. 
Then we also have some functionality in `joinable.join` that completes this PR that allows us to recoonnect with the orphaned user, should the user want their access to the account again.

The testing situatuation you asked for me to address is as follow. 
- You (thank you) created the identity deactivation test to test that pathway. 
- Surprisingly the existing `deactivate` test in `user_test.rb` is not testing the `identity: nil` statement . So the existing test actually covers the full functionality of my proposed changes in `user.deactivate` as it is. So no changes are needed to this test. 
- I have created a `join reactivates a deactivated user` test  in `identity/joinable_test.rb` to test the new reactivation enhancement. I also checked that we haven't caused any existing tests to become fragile or fail.
- I have also created a `create for existing identity with deactivated user` test in `join_codes_controller` to test the `Joinable.join` call in the `join_codes_controller`, as the existing `create for existing identity` test didn't cover the functionality.

I have tried to stay within your testing methodology and patterns identified. I have run all the test locally (they passed). So I hope that helps.

> It was already in wide circulation by the time they sought to institutionalize a specific definition I happened to end up down that rabbit hole again yesterday (@dieterbe has [the best write-up I know of](https://dieter.plaetinck.be/posts/open-source-undefined-part-1-the-alternative-origin-story/)), and I found a new pre-OSI instance that I thought was particularly interesting. In the course of writing "[The Historical Case for Fair Source](https://openpath.quest/2024/the-historical-case-for-fair-source/)" a while back, I ended up contacting Frank Hecker. He's the one that wrote the original whitepaper inside of Netscape that eventually led to them publishing their source code, kicking off OSI, etc. In the course of our conversation, I convinced him to [publish the memo for the first time](https://frankhecker.com/writings/netscape-source-code/). Previously he had only published [a later version of it](https://frankhecker.com/writings/setting-up-shop/) that had been changed significantly for outside consumption. The later version is of course replete with references to open source. But check this out: the internal version, from November 11, 1997, also has a reference to "open source code"! It's in a section on competitive analysis vis-a-vis Microsoft: > Microsoft would also face a problem similar to what it faces with Java today: that its own employees, particularly Microsoft's developers, would find the new ways (open source code, etc.) more attractive to them than the old Microsoft ways. How cool is that? 😎 That said, there is only that single reference in the pre-OSI memo, vs. 305 (by my count) in the post-OSI version. Clearly, [_something_ changed in February of 1998](https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=Open+Source%2C+Free+Software&year_start=1970&year_end=2022&corpus=en&smoothing=0). Language does evolve over time, after all. In any case, the early history of the term, and the past behavior and present effectiveness of OSI as an organization, are separable questions from whether a clear definition of the software gift economy is valuable for incorporating that gift economy into larger systems.

# Bug: Card duplication when closing from Not Now

## Root Cause

When closing a card from "Not Now" using the `]` hotkey, the Turbo Stream response failed to remove the card from its source location. The `capture_card_location` method only tracked `@source_column` (nil for postponed cards) and `@was_in_stream` (false for postponed cards), leaving no condition to handle the Not Now case. This caused the card to appear in both Done and Not Now until the next page refresh.

## Fix

Thanks @andyra! I love the idea, but I think we still need to use the magic number. The default panel paddings are quite generous, so if we just subtract the current panel padding from its radius, we'll have an inner radius of 0. I experimented a bit and ended up with this: ```css --panel-inner-border-radius: max(calc(var(--panel-border-radius) - var(--panel-padding)), 0.5em); ``` This way, the radius never gets too small. If the parent panel radius is larger, it works as expected: But since that's not the case, I'm not sure if it's worth making it more complex. I didn't open a PR, but you can see the working code here: https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/compare/main...nqst:fizzy:inner-panel-dynamic-radius

Hey @andyra, it looks like there are two separate but related changes in here:

1. `Card.mentioning` selects `status: published`
2. `Search::Record.search` joins against the `cards` table to select `status: published`

I'll write separately about each.

## `Card.mentioning`

I don't think this change is necessary! Although `Card.mentioning` by itself will return cards in "draft" status, it's only called in two places.

The first call site is in `app/controllers/prompts/cards_controller.rb` (used for Lexxy card autocompletion), where it's added to a query that is already filtering for published cards:

https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/exclude-drafts-from-search-results/app/controllers/prompts/cards_controller.rb#L21-L30

```ruby
    def search_cards
      published_cards
        .mentioning(params[:filter], user: Current.user)
        .reverse_chronologically
        .limit(MAX_RESULTS)
    end

    def published_cards
      Current.user.accessible_cards.published
    end
```

The second place is in `app/models/filter.rb` (which is what's used for the "F"-hotkeyed filter bar), and that is also being added to a query that already filtering for published cards:

https://github.com/basecamp/fizzy/blob/exclude-drafts-from-search-results/app/models/filter.rb#L19-L41

```ruby
  def cards
    @cards ||= begin
      result = creator.accessible_cards.preloaded.published   # <--- "published" filter
      result = result.indexed_by(indexed_by)
      result = result.sorted_by(sorted_by)
      result = result.where(id: card_ids) if card_ids.present?
      result = result.where.missing(:not_now) unless include_not_now_cards?
      result = result.open unless include_closed_cards?
      result = result.unassigned if assignment_status.unassigned?
      result = result.assigned_to(assignees.ids) if assignees.present?
      result = result.where(creator_id: creators.ids) if creators.present?
      result = result.where(board: boards.ids) if boards.present?
      result = result.tagged_with(tags.ids) if tags.present?
      result = result.where(cards: { created_at: creation_window }) if creation_window
      result = result.closed_at_window(closure_window) if closure_window
      result = result.closed_by(closers) if closers.present?
      result = terms.reduce(result) do |result, term|
        result.mentioning(term, user: creator)               # <--- Card.mentioning
      end

      result.distinct
    end
  end
```

So I think this is an unnecessary change -- I don't think there's any way to get draft cards to show up in the "F"-hotkeyed filter bar or the Lexxy autocomplete prompt.

## `Search::Record.search`

Here we do have a problem, and draft cards do show up in the "K"-hotkey search bar.

One way to fix this is to filter for card status at search time, which is what this change implements. And it works (although it doesn't have test coverage yet). But I'm not sure I like that we are introducing a new join against the `cards` table -- the search query previously just hits the `search_records` table.

I may be overly paranoid about search performance and maybe this is fine; but I do think we would benefit from keeping the search queries as simple as possible.

So two potential alternatives:

1. We could add the card `status` to the search table. One possible advantage here is that drafts are in the search index if we every want to do something with them; but this seems like an unlikely feature and I think YAGNI.
2. We could delay indexing cards until publish time, so the search index *only* contains published cards.

I'm leaning towards option 2 here, which is about the same complexity (in my imagination) but feels a bit cleaner to me. WDYT?

**Impact:** unlikely impact — but fizzy has relevant schema
**Matched in:**

```
  <form id="passkey-form" method="POST" action="/my/passkeys">
    <input type="hidden" name="authenticity_token" value="<%= form_authenticity_token %>">
    <input type="hidden" name="passkey[client_data_json]" id="passkey-client-data-json">
    <input type="hidden" name="passkey[attestation_object]" id="passkey-attestation-object">
    <input type="hidden" name="passkey[transports]" id="passkey-transports">

    <button type="button" onclick="createPasskey()">Register a passkey</button>
  </form>
```

This needs to boil down to a html helper, like:

```
<%= button_to_create_passkey "Register a passkey" %>
```

And:

```
  <script type="module">
    import { register } from "lib/action_pack/webauthn"

    const publicKey = <%= @creation_options.to_json.html_safe %>

    window.createPasskey = async function() {
      const passkey = await register(publicKey)

      document.getElementById("passkey-client-data-json").value = passkey.client_data_json
      document.getElementById("passkey-attestation-object").value = passkey.attestation_object
      document.getElementById("passkey-transports").value = JSON.stringify(passkey.transports)

      document.getElementById("passkey-form").submit()
    }
  </script>
```

Needs to boil down to something like:

```
<%= passkey_public_key_meta_tag(@creation_options) %>
```

Which sets the publicKey to a `<meta name="passkey-public-key" content="#{creation_options.to_json.html_safe}">` or the like. Then the window.createPasskey function has to be added by a generic script that can reference that meta field. We should not be generating a blob of JavaScript code that lives in the root of the document.

We can also boil this down:

```ruby
  class PasskeysController < ApplicationController
    def new
      @creation_options = ActionPack::WebAuthn::Passkey.creation_options(holder: Current.identity)
      session[:webauthn_challenge] = @creation_options.challenge
    end

    def create
      Current.identity.passkeys.register(
        passkey: params.expect(passkey: [ :client_data_json, :attestation_object, transports: [] ]),
        challenge: session.delete(:webauthn_challenge)
      )

      redirect_to root_path
    rescue ActionPack::WebAuthn::InvalidAuthenticationResponseError => error
      render json: { error: error.message }, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end
```

to:

```ruby
  class PasskeysController < ApplicationController
    def new
      @passkey_creation_options = passkey_creation_options(holder: Current.identity)
      session[:webauthn_challenge] = @creation_options.challenge
    end

    def create
      # The generic rescue is done in a rescue_from via the include in ActionController.
      Current.identity.passkeys.register(passkey: passkey_params, challenge: session.delete(:webauthn_challenge))
      redirect_to root_path
    end
  end
```

Also, we need to make `ActionPack::Passkeys` the top-level scope anyone on the user-facing side are dealing with. WebAuthn is an implementational detail that shouldn't leak into user-land. What people care about are passkeys, so that's what the entire API should be focused on.

This is a low-risk patch upgrade. Of the 12 commits, 11 touch only CI workflows (`.github/`), gemspec packaging metadata, `NEWS.md`, or `lib/erb/version.rb` — none change runtime behavior. The single runtime change is a security-hardening guard on `ERB#def_method` that only affects ERB instances reconstructed via `Marshal.load`, a pattern Fizzy does not use.

## Analyzed — No App Impact

### 9d017be4: Prohibit `def_method` on marshal-loaded ERB instances

**Impact:** unlikely impact

`ERB#def_method` now raises `ArgumentError, "not initialized"` unless `@_init` matches the instance singleton class. `def_module` and `def_class` delegate to `def_method` and are covered by the same guard. This blocks `eval` of arbitrary `src` on an ERB object created via `Marshal.load` (which bypasses `initialize`).

**Searched and NOT matched in fizzy:**

- App ERB usage is limited to `ERB::Util.html_escape` (`app/helpers/html_helper.rb:9`), the `ERB::Util` mixin (`app/models/event/description.rb:3`, `app/models/card/eventable/system_commenter.rb:2`), and `ERB.new(...).result` (`config/database.yml:9`, `config/storage.yml:9`). None call `def_method`/`def_module`/`def_class`, and none marshal ERB instances.
- Gem dependencies (173 lib/app dirs): no `ERB#def_method`/`def_module`/`def_class` calls. The `parser` and `prism` gems contain `builder.def_method`/`def_class`/`def_module` calls, but those operate on AST builder objects, not ERB instances — false positives.
- No `Marshal.load`/`Marshal.dump` of ERB instances anywhere in app or dependencies.

Marcel is a **transitive dependency** in fizzy, pulled in via ActiveStorage (`marcel (~> 1.0)`). Fizzy has **no direct references** to `Marcel::` (confirmed: only `Gemfile.lock` mentions it). It is exercised indirectly: ActiveStorage calls `Marcel::MimeType.for(io, name:, declared_type:)`, `Marcel::Magic.new`, `Marcel::Magic.child?`, and `Marcel::Magic.by_extension` when identifying/serving attachments.

**Public API is unchanged** across this range. The entire public surface (`Marcel::MimeType.for`/`.extend`, `Marcel::Magic.new`/`.by_magic`/`.by_path`/`.by_extension`/`.child?`/`.add`/`.remove`/`.extend`) is identical between v1.1.0 and v1.2.1. `Marcel::Magic.remove` already existed in v1.1.0 — it is not new.

The changes in this range are (a) MIME-type detection-table data updates and (b) a new internal regexp magic-match mechanism. `MimeType.for` always runs magic-byte detection first and prefers it over the declared type, so changed detection rules *can* alter the content type assigned to an upload. However, none of the changed detections intersect the content types fizzy actually accepts or references.

### Fizzy's attachment surface (the only way marcel runs)

- `User::Avatar::ALLOWED_AVATAR_CONTENT_TYPES = %w[image/jpeg image/png image/gif image/webp]` (`app/models/user/avatar.rb:6`) — magic for jpeg/png/gif/webp is **unchanged** in this range.

- `Export#file`, `Account::Import#file`, `ZipFile` all use an explicit `content_type: "application/zip"` (`app/models/export.rb:5`, `app/models/zip_file.rb:38,51,79`) — zip magic is **unchanged**.
- `Identity#avatar` (`app/models/identity.rb:12`).

No fizzy code references `text/html`, `image/svg`, `application/x-bzip2`, `audio/ogg`, `audio/mpeg`, `text/markdown`, `image/bmp`, `application/pkcs8`, `application/gpx+xml`, or `image/x-raw-sony` as content-type strings (the `content-type^=` references in `attachments.css`/`lexxy.css` and `account/seeder.rb` are ActionText attachment HTML attributes, unrelated to marcel detection).

**nokogiri v1.19.4 is a pure security release.** It bundles 9 security advisories (8 CRuby, 1 JRuby), all low/medium severity and all backwards-compatible hardening. | `app/models/webhook/delivery.rb` | 158 | `Nokogiri::HTML5(html)` then `.css`, `.replace`, `.text` | No — HTML5 parse + CSS traversal; none of the patched APIs. |

### Test-only call sites (all safe)

`Nokogiri::HTML.fragment` / `Nokogiri::HTML5` / `Nokogiri::HTML::DocumentFragment.parse` / `Nokogiri::HTML5.fragment` + `.at_css`, `.children` in `test/controllers/cards/comments_controller_test.rb`, `test/helpers/application_helper_test.rb`, `test/mailers/notification/bundle_mailer_test.rb`, `test/test_helpers/action_text_test_helper.rb`, `test/system/markdown_paste_test.rb`. All are parse + read paths; none exercise an affected API.

### Transitive `Document#encoding=` call sites (all safe)

The `Document#encoding=` UAF (GHSA-5v8h-3h3q-446p) only triggers when the *setter itself raises* an exception. The only call sites anywhere in fizzy's dependency tree are the standard parse-time assignments in loofah and actiontext, and **all pass a valid `String`**, so the setter never raises and the UAF path is never reached:

- `loofah/lib/loofah/concerns.rb:175` — `doc.encoding = encoding` (a String: `tags.encoding.name` or `"UTF-8"`).
- `loofah/lib/loofah/xml/document_fragment.rb:14` — `doc.encoding = tags.encoding.name if tags.respond_to?(:encoding)` (a String).
- `actiontext/lib/action_text/html_conversion.rb:23` — `doc.encoding = "UTF-8"` (a String literal).

These are the encoding assignments Rails/loofah perform on every fragment parse. No mitigation needed.

(Note: the three `\.encoding =` matches inside fizzy's own `lib/action_pack/web_authn/**` are `String#encoding == Encoding::BINARY` comparisons, not `Nokogiri::XML::Document#encoding=`. Unrelated.)

1. **Update the OSS lockfile.** Run `bundle update --conservative nokogiri` so `Gemfile.lock` resolves nokogiri (and all platform variants) to `1.19.4`. Confirm the lockfile no longer references `1.19.3`. *(Done — all 8 platform variants moved 1.19.3 → 1.19.4; no transitive dependency changed.)*
2. **Sync the SaaS lockfile.** fizzy maintains a second lockfile, `Gemfile.saas.lock` (the SaaS Gemfile `eval`s the OSS Gemfile, so shared gems must match). `bin/bundle-drift check` (a `bin/ci` step) fails if the two drift. Run `bin/bundle-drift forward` to push the nokogiri bump into `Gemfile.saas.lock`. *(Done — all 8 variants in `Gemfile.saas.lock` moved 1.19.3 → 1.19.4 via a spec-version patch; `bin/bundle-drift check` now reports the lockfiles in sync. Do **not** run `bin/bundle-drift correct` here — that treats the SaaS lock as authoritative and would revert the OSS bump back to 1.19.3.)*
3. **Recompile and test.** Run `bin/setup`, then `bin/ci`. No code or test changes are expected.
4. **Verify.** Tests should pass with no behavior change. Because fizzy calls none of the patched libxml2 APIs in a way the fixes alter, and the only transitive `Document#encoding=` call sites pass valid Strings, no test or code changes are required.

### Bump mechanics (Fizzy dual-lockfile)

Conservative update of all 12 rails component gems moved **only rails** — zero transitive-dep changes. `Gemfile.saas.lock` updated first (`bundle update --conservative rails <components>`), then `Gemfile.lock` seeded from it and re-locked (revision-level sync; `bin/bundle-drift check` only compares versions, which are identically `8.2.0.alpha`, so it can't detect git-revision drift on its own).

### Code changes required (3 — all missed by static analysis, caught by tests)

The plan predicted "0 mandatory" changes; the test suite surfaced three real edge-API breaks:

1. **`http_cache_forever` `last_modified:` keyword** (actionpack `048683577c` + Active Storage blob proxy now passing `last_modified: @blob.created_at`). Fizzy's `ActiveStorage::Authorize#http_cache_forever(public:, &block)` override rejected the new keyword → `ArgumentError`. Fix: forward `**options` to super. *(lib/rails_ext/active_storage_authorization.rb)*
2. **Active Storage after-destroy callback rename** (activestorage `bae458450a`: `purge_dependent_blob_later` → `purge_dependent_blob`, now also handling `dependent: :purge`). Fizzy's purge-on-last-attachment override targeted the old name → dead code → a `PurgeJob` enqueued for still-shared blobs. Fix: override the new name, mirror the `:purge`/`:purge_later` contract, keep the last-attachment guard. *(config/initializers/active_storage_purge_on_last_attachment.rb)*
3. **Sentry × Action Cable connection refactor** (actioncable `647ce6769c`: WebSocket handling extracted to `ActionCable::Server::Socket`, which now calls `connection.handle_open`/`handle_close` **publicly**). sentry-rails ≤6.6.2/master still prepends these as `private` → `NoMethodError`, every WebSocket connection dies. **SaaS-only** (Sentry ships only in the SaaS Gemfile — the reason OSS system tests passed but SaaS's failed). Fix: an `on_load(:action_cable_connection)` hook restoring public visibility on Sentry's module. Remove once sentry-ruby adapts. *(saas/lib/fizzy/saas/engine.rb)*

Why static analysis missed all three: (1)/(2) the recon commits were classified against Fizzy's *direct* Active Storage usage, not its *overrides* of Active Storage/Action Controller internals whose signatures changed; (3) the break lives in a transitive gem (sentry-rails), not Rails or Fizzy code, and only manifests through the runtime WebSocket path. Feeds a practice-gap note for `upgrade-analyze`: flag app overrides of framework-internal methods (`http_cache_forever`, `purge_dependent_blob*`, Action Cable connection lifecycle) and known monkeypatching gems (sentry-rails, yabeda) when their upstream signatures/visibility change.

    attributes on jobs. Attribute values are automatically included in the
    serialized job data and restored on deserialization, eliminating the need
    to manually override `serialize` and `deserialize`.

    This is especially useful with `ActiveJob::Continuable`, where a job may be
    interrupted and resumed and attributes are preserved across resumptions.

    ```ruby

      attribute :payment_token, :string
      attribute :billing_profile_id, :integer

        end
    ```

## Active Storage (17 entries)

*   Fix `MirrorService#mirror` losing blob metadata when copying to mirrors.

    Mirrored copies on S3, Azure, and GCS were served as `application/octet-stream`
    because `content_type`, `filename`, `disposition`, and `custom_metadata` were
    dropped. Forward the blob's `service_metadata` to each mirror's upload.

    Fixes #57270.

    *Maksim Romanov* + *Andrii Furmanets*

*   Offload ActiveStorage::Blob#metadata sync to background

    Problem:

    A data race can occur when both a http server and a background worker (
    `ActiveStorage::AnalyzeJob`) attempt to update a blob's metadata
    simultaneously. This leads to a 409 conflict on GCS.

    Solution:

    Offload the metadata upload to a background job so the 409 no longer breaks
    the request with a 500. Applications can add `retry_on` to
    `ActiveStorage::SyncMetadataJob` to retry the conflict for their service.

    `ActiveStorage::Service#update_metadata` now instruments the work and
    delegates it to a new `update_metadata_for` method. Custom services that
    overrode `update_metadata` should override `update_metadata_for` instead, so
    the work runs inside the instrumentation.

    *Shouichi Kamiya*

    ImageProcessing 2.0 now requires adding `ruby-vips` or `mini_magick` gems explicitly to the Gemfile.

    *Janko Marohnić*

    When `ActiveStorage.touch_attachment_records` was set to `false`, attaching a existing Blob to a Record
    would raise an error. This is now fixed.

    *Edouard Chin*

*   Parallelize `exist?` checks and uploads in `MirrorService#mirror` using
    the existing internal thread pool. With N mirrors, wall time drops from
    O(N) to O(1) network round-trips for both phases.

    `ActiveStorage::AnalyzeJob` writes only to `Blob#metadata`. The cascade
    that touches attached records (and their parents) exists for cache-key
    invalidation; when those records use optimistic locking, the previous
    behavior bumped `lock_version`, causing concurrent form edits to raise
    spurious `ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError`s. The `updated_at` cascade is
    preserved; the `lock_version` bump on this code path is now suppressed.

    Fixes #55764.

loofah 2.25.2 is a coordinated security release shipping three backwards-compatible
sanitizer hardening fixes (data: URI / PROTOCOL_SEPARATOR, SVG `href` restriction
[GHSA-9wjq-cp2p-hrgf](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-9wjq-cp2p-hrgf),

## How loofah reaches fizzy

The analysis confirmed two paths, neither of which requires code changes:

1. **Action Text (the real sanitization surface).** fizzy declares `has_rich_text`

   sanitization routes through `rails-html-sanitizer` →
   `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?`, so the `allowed_uri?` and protocol fixes
   land here automatically. The app's sanitizer allowlist customization lives in
   `config/initializers/sanitization.rb`, which extends
   `Rails::HTML5::SafeListSanitizer` with tags `s, table, tr, td, th, thead, tbody,
   details, summary, video, source` and attributes `data-turbo-frame,
   data-lightbox-target, data-lightbox-caption-value, controls, type, width`. It
   adds no SVG elements and no `href`-family attributes, so the SVG `href`
   restriction has no allowlisted surface to act on.

2. **Custom scrubber (orthogonal).** `lib/auto_link_scrubber.rb` defines
   `AutoLinkScrubber < Loofah::Scrubber`, invoked at `app/helpers/html_helper.rb:3`.
   It is a text-node auto-linker that wraps plain `http`/`https` URLs and email
   addresses (`URI::DEFAULT_PARSER.make_regexp(%w[http https])`, `mailto:`) and
   generates its own `href` values. It never calls `allowed_uri?`, reads no
   protocol allowlist, and handles no SVG. It is unaffected by every change in the

This is a coordinated security patch release. It is applied together with the loofah 2.25.2 bump (analyzed in parallel). The substantive change is [PR #223](https://github.com/rails/rails-html-sanitizer/pull/223) (`svg-href-local-ref`, commit 74dcb805): rails-html-sanitizer independently reimplements the SVG local-href restriction, and where 1.7.0 covered only `xlink:href`, 1.7.1 extends it to plain `href`, closing the plain-`href` half of [GHSA-9wjq-cp2p-hrgf](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9wjq-cp2p-hrgf) on the Rails `sanitize`/Action Text path.

**Bottom line for fizzy:** the vulnerable code path is present and reachable through the general `sanitize`/Action Text plumbing, but the specific behavior change has **no observable effect** on fizzy's sanitized output, because `svg` is never in fizzy's sanitizer allowlist. The whole `<svg>` subtree is stripped by the tag allowlist before the widened `href`/`xlink:href` gate is ever reached. The upgrade should still proceed as a security-hygiene / dependency-floor fix, and it is **lockfile-only** — no fizzy application code changes are required.

## Commits Requiring Mitigation

Both entries below drive one and the same action: the coordinated lockfile bump. Neither requires an application-code change.

### 74dcb805: Properly restrict SVG href attributes (PR #223)

**Impact:** likely impact (recon) → **inert-but-present** (fizzy)

**What changed upstream:** `PermitScrubber#scrub_attribute` reimplements Loofah's SVG local-reference restriction. Before this commit the restriction gated only on the literal attribute name `xlink:href`; SVG 2 also permits a plain `href`, so `<use href="https://evil.example/x.svg#p"/>` bypassed the local-only check. The commit replaces the `attr_name == "xlink:href"` test with a membership check against `Loofah::HTML5::SafeList::SVG_HREF_ATTRIBUTES` (a constant introduced in loofah 2.25.2).

**Reachable but inert in fizzy:**
- `config/initializers/sanitization.rb:2-7` is fizzy's entire sanitizer customization. It merges block/inline/media tags (`s`, `table`, `tr`, `td`, `th`, `thead`, `tbody`, `details`, `summary`, `video`, `source`, plus `figure`/`figcaption` for Action Text) and a few Turbo/lightbox data attributes (`data-turbo-frame`, `data-lightbox-target`, `data-lightbox-caption-value`, `controls`, `type`, `width`). It adds **no** `svg`, `use`, `image`, `feImage`, `pattern`, `filter`, or gradient element, and no `xlink:href` attribute.
- The base `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TAGS` fizzy merges into contains only prose/inline tags — no SVG elements.
- `ActionText::ContentHelper` derives its allowlist from the same svg-free set; `ContentHelper.scrubber` is left `nil`, so Action Text uses the stock `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` — no custom subclass. App-wide search found only `lib/auto_link_scrubber.rb` (`AutoLinkScrubber`), which auto-links plain URLs/emails in already-sanitized text nodes and never touches attribute scrubbing.
- User-content Action Text fields that flow through the scrubber: `Card#has_rich_text :description` (`app/models/card.rb:13`), `Comment#has_rich_text :body` (`app/models/comment.rb:9`), `Board#has_rich_text :public_description` (`app/models/board.rb:7`). Because `svg` is not an allowed element, any `<svg>` in this content is stripped whole before `scrub_attribute`'s href gate runs.
- All SVG that does render in fizzy is trusted, developer-authored template markup that never passes through `sanitize`: inline brand/decoration SVG (`app/views/cards/display/preview/_bubble.html.erb`, `app/views/layouts/public.html.erb`, `app/views/my/_menu.html.erb`), server-rendered initials avatars (`app/views/users/avatars/show.svg.erb`, `Users::AvatarsController#render_initials`), and QR codes (`QrCodesController`).
- A separate SVG-file-upload avatar path (served via ActiveStorage `rails_blob_path`) is not parsed by `rails-html-sanitizer` at all — a different vulnerability class (stored SVG content-type serving), out of scope for this commit.

**Conclusion:** the widened attribute-name check never runs against attacker-controlled input in fizzy, because SVG tags are stripped upstream of it. The upgrade still closes the vulnerability in the general case and is worth adopting.

**Mitigation:**
- Upgrade rails-html-sanitizer to the release carrying this commit (1.7.1) and allow Bundler to bump `loofah` to `>= 2.25.2` (pulls in `crass` 1.0.7 as a transitive bump per the lockfile). No configuration change is required.
- If any test fixtures assert that external plain-`href` SVG references survive sanitization, update those expectations: the attribute is now removed, which is the intended, safer behavior. (None found in fizzy's current tests.)
- Review any custom `PermitScrubber` subclass; if it reimplements the SVG href check with `attr_name == "xlink:href"`, update it to gate on `Loofah::HTML5::SafeList::SVG_HREF_ATTRIBUTES`. (Fizzy has no such subclass.)

I dug into the PDF attachment half of this and could not reproduce it. Sharing what I ruled out, plus the one piece of information that would settle it.

**The error is an upload request failure, not a file type filter.** The "Error uploading MEDICARE_SELECT.pdf" box is Lexxy's `createDOMForError()`, which is only reachable from the `DirectUpload#create` error callback. So the POST or the storage PUT failed. Nothing inspected the file and decided to reject it.

What I checked and cleared:

- **No content type allowlist applies here.** `ALLOWED_AVATAR_CONTENT_TYPES` governs avatars only. Lexxy's client-side `permittedAttachmentTypes` defaults to permit-all, and Fizzy never calls `Lexxy.configure`, so it is inactive.
- **`config/initializers/vips.rb` is not involved.** It subtracts only bmp, ico, and psd from `variable_content_types`, and `application/pdf` was never in that list.
- **The one PDF-specific server branch is safe.** Lexxy prepends `ActiveStorage::BlobWithPreviewUrl`, so `blob.as_json` calls `preview(...)` when `previewable?`, and among jpg/docx/pdf only PDF is previewable. This was my main suspect. It returns 200 both when a previewer is present and when it is absent, which matters because the Dockerfile installs libvips but no poppler, so deployed instances have no PDF previewer.
- **Not a size or infrastructure gate.** There is no byte-size or quota check in app code, and Thruster's `MAX_REQUEST_BODY` defaults to unlimited.

Repro attempts, all successful, dropping files into the real editor in a headless browser: a real 1.9 MB multi-page PDF, a small synthetic PDF, a DOCX, and a JPG. Zero errors, clean console, correct `<action-text-attachment>` in every case, with the PDF carrying `previewable="true"`. I also re-ran all four against lexxy 0.9.14.beta, the version pinned when this was filed, in case the 0.9.23 bump was relevant. Also clean.

**What would settle it:** could you open DevTools, retry the PDF, and share the failed request's HTTP status, plus the file size? Lexxy also logs a console line whose wording identifies which leg failed, "Error creating Blob..." for the POST versus "Error storing..." for the PUT. Either one would immediately narrow this down.

Two things I could not check that may matter: whether your DOCX upload happened in the same session as the PDF failure (in the screenshot it looks like an already-saved attachment rather than a fresh upload, and if so the type contrast may be coincidental), and what storage service and reverse proxy your instance runs.

One unrelated thing I noticed while tracing this, in case it applies to your setup: `config/initializers/content_security_policy.rb` sets `connect_src :self` with no S3 host. If you run with `ACTIVE_STORAGE_SERVICE=s3` and have not set `CSP_CONNECT_SRC`, the browser would block every direct upload PUT and produce this exact error box. That would fail for all file types rather than PDFs specifically, so it does not match your report, but it is worth ruling out.

holding trace propagation headers, whether or not tracing is enabled.

`false` (`saas/lib/fizzy/saas/engine.rb:83`). No user data enters job payloads.

**Rolling-deploy safety: confirmed safe in both directions.**
- Old payload (no `_sentry` key) read by the new gem: `deserialize`
  (line 55-64) assigns `nil`; `perform_now` (line 18-28) does `data = _sentry || {}`.
- New payload (with `_sentry`) read by the old gem: 6.2.0 has no `deserialize`
  override, and ActiveJob core reads only its known keys. The extra key is inert.
- Both `serialize` and `deserialize` wrap their work in `rescue StandardError`.

**Mitigation:**
Decide explicitly whether to accept the payload change. Two options:

1. **Accept it** (recommended if you may enable tracing later). No code change.
   Job payloads grow by roughly one hash with a `sentry-trace` and a `baggage`
   string per job.
2. **Opt out**, keeping payloads byte-identical:
   ```ruby
   config.rails.active_job_propagate_traces = false
   ```
   Add this to the `Sentry.init` block in `saas/lib/fizzy/saas/engine.rb`.

Either way, no rollback coordination is needed for in-flight Solid Queue jobs.

### a1c52820: `mechanism.handled` now reflects the real `handled:` flag

**Impact:** likely impact — **this is the motivating fix for the upgrade**

Present in the 6.7.0 tree, first released in 6.5.0. Upstream
`sentry-rails/lib/sentry/rails/error_subscriber.rb` gained
`hint[:mechanism] ||= Sentry::Mechanism.new(type: Sentry::Rails.integration_name, handled: handled)`.
Before the fix, `hint[:mechanism]` was never populated, so
`Sentry::Client#capture_event` fell back to `Mechanism.new`, and every error
from the Rails error subscriber was badged with the fallback value regardless of
what Rails passed.

**No app-side config or code change is needed for the fix to take effect.**
`config.rails.register_error_subscriber = true` is already set at
`saas/lib/fizzy/saas/engine.rb:88`, so `Sentry::Rails::ErrorSubscriber` is
already registered. The fix applies on gem upgrade alone.

**Measured before and after.** `tmp/verify_handled.rb` in the fizzy worktree
inits Sentry against a capturing `before_send`, subscribes
`Sentry::Rails::ErrorSubscriber`, reports three errors, and prints each event's
`mechanism.handled`. Run once per lockfile:

| `Rails.error.report` argument | 6.2.0 | 6.7.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `handled: true` | `false` | `true` |
| `handled: false` | `false` | `false` |
| omitted (Rails defaults to `true`) | `false` | `true` |

At 6.2.0 the mechanism reads `false` in every case, including when Rails'
default supplies `handled: true`.

**Report sites, with the actual net change:**
- `app/jobs/search_reindex_job.rb:54` —
  `Rails.error.report(e, context: { record_type: ..., record_id: ... })`. No
  explicit `handled:`, so ActiveSupport's default `handled: true` applies.
  **Flips from unhandled to handled.**
- `app/models/signup.rb:35` — `Rails.error.report(error, severity: :error)`.
  Same. **Flips from unhandled to handled.**
- No `Rails.error.handle` or `Rails.error.record` call sites exist anywhere in
  `app/`, `lib/`, `test/`, `config/`, or `saas/`.

So the fix is live for fizzy, not prospective: both existing report sites change
classification. It additionally corrects any future `Rails.error.record` call
and `retry_on`/`discard_on` with `report: true`, which the initializer comment
at line 87 says fizzy relies on.

Note that neither test suite covers this. The `fizzy_saas.sentry` initializer is
gated on `!Rails.env.local?`, so Sentry never boots under test. Green suites
show the upgrade broke nothing; they are not evidence the fix works.

**Mitigation:**
1. Upgrade the gems. Nothing else is required.
2. After deploy, spot-check a few Sentry issues sourced from the Rails error
   reporter and confirm `mechanism.handled` reads correctly.
3. Review any Sentry alert rule or dashboard filtering on `handled` — issue
   classification from `retry_on`/`discard_on` reports shifts after this upgrade.

🤖 Reviewed this bump against [`docs/8.0-Upgrade.md`](https://github.com/puma/puma/blob/master/docs/8.0-Upgrade.md), taking each flagged behavior as a lens on our config and deploy.

Six of the seven don't apply — `before_thread_start`, `supported_http_methods`, `http_content_length_limit`, `fork_worker`, explicit `[::]`/`ssl_bind` binds, and any SIGPWR or `pumactl info` wiring are all absent from the app, `saas/`, the workflows, and the Kamal configs. The hooks `config/puma.rb` does use — `before_fork`, `before_worker_boot`, `out_of_band` — still exist in 8.0.2, and they're blocks, so the new hook arity can't raise `ArgumentError`.

The default bind is the one that reaches us. `config/puma.rb` sets `port` with no host, so we inherit puma's new default — but that default is resolved at boot, not hardcoded:

```ruby
# puma-8.0.2/lib/puma/configuration.rb:369
def self.default_tcp_host
  ipv6_interface_available? ? Const::UNSPECIFIED_IPV6 : Const::UNSPECIFIED_IPV4
end
```

Running that predicate inside a container returns false — only `::1` shows up in `/proc/net/if_inet6` — so we bind `0.0.0.0` exactly as puma 7 did. Where a host does expose a non-loopback IPv6, `[::]` under `net.ipv6.bindv6only=0` still accepts IPv4, Thruster dials `http://localhost:%d`, and `Puma::Client#socket_peerip` calls `unmap_ipv6`, so `REMOTE_ADDR` stays IPv4-shaped for v4 clients. Nothing downstream parses a bare `HOST:PORT`. The metrics endpoint is unaffected: `yabeda-prometheus-mmap` runs its own WEBrick on `PROMETHEUS_EXPORTER_BIND || '0.0.0.0'`, independent of puma's bind.

Confirmed empirically — deployed to staging and exercised in development, IPv6 behavior fine in both.

One dev-only nit, out of scope here: `config/environments/development.rb` omits `::1` from `config.hosts`, so a bare `bin/rails server` reached over `http://[::1]:3000` would 403. `Procfile.dev` pins `-b 0.0.0.0`, so the usual path never hits it.

**Verdict: good to merge once `CI (SaaS)` is green on this head.** Worth watching that specifically — the earlier `CI (SaaS): success` on this branch ran on `3c6fd7f6`, whose `Gemfile.saas.lock` still pinned `puma (7.2.0)`. The sync commit that brought the SaaS lock to 8.0.2 was pushed with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which doesn't trigger workflows, so until this push the test matrix had never seen puma 8 in SaaS mode.

## Database constraints — the specific concern

Mike suspected a constraint-related behavior change in this range. **There is one, and it is real, but it is not in the constraint DDL or schema-dumping code — it is in `ae739c38`, and it manifests as primary-key `NOT NULL` violations.** Details in the first mitigation entry below.

Everything in the constraint/schema-reader surface proper was checked and ruled out:

| Area | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Batched schema readers (`431ba5cf`, `706a5645`, `23bb4cdd`, `2cb3daba`) changing `db/schema.rb` output | **Ruled out.** `SchemaDumper` sorts index, FK, and check-constraint statements before printing (`schema_dumper.rb:278-296`, `:327-338`, `:351-378`), so the new SQLite top-level queries lacking `ORDER BY` cannot reorder the dump. Column order is still pinned by `ORDER BY m.name, t.cid`. |
| Fizzy's check constraints / foreign keys | **None to break.** `db/schema.rb` and `db/schema_sqlite.rb` contain zero `t.check_constraint`/`add_check_constraint` and zero `add_foreign_key`. The only FKs in the repo are 6 in `db/queue_schema.rb` (Solid Queue). |
| MySQL `information_schema.columns` switch + `unquote_mariadb_default` (`23bb4cdd`) | **Ruled out.** `unquote_mariadb_default` is gated on `mariadb?`; fizzy runs real MySQL 8.4. No string defaults in `db/schema.rb` contain quotes, backslashes, or newlines. ## Commits Requiring Mitigation

### ae739c38: Extract model schema state into a schema context

**Impact:** definite

`ActiveRecord::ModelSchema` moves schema-derived state into a new per-class `SchemaContext`. The new `ClassMethods#load_schema` (`model_schema.rb:557-571`) runs:

1. `context = build_schema_context` — a **new** hook, `model_schema.rb:209`, which does not exist at `ce95deb7`
2. `context.load_schema!` — computes and caches `@default_attributes` via `model_class.apply_pending_attribute_modifications(attribute_set)`
3. `load_schema!` — the model's own hook, now running **after** step 2

**Matched in:**
- `config/initializers/uuid_primary_keys.rb:4` (at `HEAD`) — `UuidPrimaryKeyDefault#load_schema!` prepends onto `ActiveRecord::Base` and appends a `PendingUuidDefault` to `pending_attribute_modifications` before calling `super`.

At `HEAD` this hook fires at step 3, after the default attributes have already been computed and cached at step 2. The UUID primary-key default generator becomes **silently inert** — no boot error, just `nil` primary keys on `INSERT`, surfacing as primary-key / `NOT NULL` constraint violations. This is the database-constraint behavior change in the range.

**Mitigation:**

Move the hook from `load_schema!` to `build_schema_context`, so it runs at step 1:

```ruby
module UuidPrimaryKeyDefault
  # Rails builds the schema context's attribute set (applying pending attribute
  # modifications) inside `load_schema`, before the model's own `load_schema!`
  # hook runs, so the default has to be registered as the context is built.
  def build_schema_context
    define_uuid_primary_key_pending_default
    super
  end
```

Add a regression test asserting a fresh model gets a generated UUID PK, so this fails loudly rather than in production.

**Already applied in the working tree**, along with `test/models/uuid_primary_key_test.rb` (untracked) covering exactly this. Verified by tracing the new `model_schema.rb` / `schema_context.rb` call order: `build_schema_context` runs before `SchemaContext#load_schema!`, so the pending modification is in place when `apply_pending_attribute_modifications` reads it. Correct.

Secondary note from the assessment: this commit also marks `SchemaContext` as not-yet-Ractor-shareable (upstream skipped two tests). Irrelevant on Ruby 3.4.8.

---

### baa1ca5f: Freeze the Controller `default_url_options`

**Impact:** definite

`ActionDispatch::Routing::UrlFor`'s class-level `default_url_options` changes from `{}` to `{}.freeze`. In-place mutation now raises `FrozenError`.

**Matched in** (all test-only; production code only reads or reassigns wholesale):
- `test/test_helper.rb:78` — `integration_session.default_url_options[:script_name] = ...` (`IntegrationTest` setup)
- `test/test_helper.rb:95` — `self.default_url_options[:script_name] = ...` (`SystemTestCase` setup)
- `test/test_helpers/session_test_helper.rb:56` — `... [:script_name] = ""`
- `test/test_helpers/session_test_helper.rb:59` — restore in `ensure`
- `test/controllers/controller_authentication_test.rb:6` — `... [:script_name] = "" # no tenant`

Every fizzy integration and system test sets `script_name` for the account-slug prefix, so this breaks the whole suite, not a corner of it.

**Mitigation:**

Replace in-place mutation with whole-hash reassignment, matching what Rails' own suite adopted in the same commit:

```ruby
integration_session.default_url_options =
  integration_session.default_url_options.merge(script_name: "...")
```

For `session_test_helper.rb#untenanted`, capture the whole hash and restore it wholesale rather than restoring one key.

**Already applied in the working tree** at all five sites.

Notes on the non-obvious ones:

- **38efca8d** — no call site in fizzy uses the `relation.update(id, attrs)` form; every `.update`/`.update!` is a single-argument instance call. Fizzy is not exposed to the cross-tenant hole, and the tightened scoping is free.

- **All eight Ractor/freeze commits** — fizzy is on Ruby 3.4.8, where `ActiveSupport::Ractors.make_shareable` is a no-op shim, and fizzy never sets `unshareable_proc_action` nor uses `Ractor` at all.

## Commits Requiring Mitigation

### 0f9f5e31: Classify `ImageProcessing::Error` as `unreadable` in `MagickOperation` and `VipsOperation`

**Impact:** likely impact

`ImageProcessing::Error` — the pipeline's own refusal of an input against the requested
transform, e.g. a multi-layer source into a single-layer destination — was unclassified and
fell through to a generic `failed` verdict, which is transient. So a file the pipeline had
already refused was reconverted on every future request, indefinitely. It is now `unreadable`
and permanent.

**Matched in:**

- `/home/flavorjones/Work/basecamp/fizzy--dep-hotcell-0.3.1/saas/lib/fizzy/saas/cell.rb:59` —
  `permanent: UnprocessableAttachment, transient: ProcessingUnavailable`. This is the whole
  exposure: fizzy maps the verdict generically and never names `ImageProcessing::Error`. A
  failure that arrived as `ProcessingUnavailable` (retried forever) now arrives as
  `UnprocessableAttachment`, which `saas/lib/fizzy/saas/unprocessable_attachments.rb`
  discards once, reports to Sentry at `:info`, marks the blob, and answers 422.
- `/home/flavorjones/Work/basecamp/fizzy--dep-hotcell-0.3.1/saas/test/lib/yabeda/hot_cell_test.rb:115` —
  metrics are keyed on the hotcell code, so volume shifts from `failed` into `unreadable`.
- Zero references to `ImageProcessing` anywhere in fizzy outside the gem.

**Mitigation:**

Bump the gems. No application code changes are required — this restores the permanent/unreadable
classification the in-process pre-hotcell path used, so it is a regression fix rather than new
behavior. After upgrading, read any dashboard or alert built on hotcell failure-classification
counts with the shift in mind: previously-`failed` incompatible-transform failures now land in
`unreadable`.

Every test that exercises the permanent/transient split
(`saas/test/models/unprocessable_attachment_test.rb`,
`saas/test/integration/unprocessable_representation_test.rb`, `saas/test/lib/cell_test.rb`,
`saas/test/lib/yabeda/hot_cell_test.rb`) stubs fizzy's own exception classes rather than raising
a real `ImageProcessing::Error` through a real cell, so none asserts the upstream classification
and none goes stale.

## Commits Requiring Mitigation

### 1bcac835 + 112bb1cb: Add batch support (and refine it)

**Impact:** definite impact (1bcac835) / likely impact (112bb1cb)

**What changed:** v1.7.0 adds `SolidQueue::Batch`, two new tables (`solid_queue_batches`, `solid_queue_batch_executions`) and a `solid_queue_jobs.batch_id` column. The recon for 1bcac835 says enqueueing on an unmigrated DB raises `ActiveModel::UnknownAttributeError`; that was true at 1bcac835 but 112bb1cb (also in v1.7.0) made the schema optional. Verified at the `v1.7.0` tag:

- `Job.attributes_from_active_job` only sets `batch_id` `if Batch.migrated?` (`app/models/solid_queue/job.rb:73`).
- `Job::Batchable#batched?` is `Batch.migrated? && batch_id?`.
- `Batch.migrated?` checks both tables and the `batch_id` column exist.
- `Dispatcher::Maintenance#sweep_stalled_batches` calls `Batch.warn_about_pending_migrations` once per dispatcher process instead of querying missing tables.
- `UPGRADING.md`: "The migration is optional for now: until you run it, everything works as before, batches aside. It will become part of the required schema in Solid Queue 2.0."

**Residual delta for fizzy:**

- `db/queue_schema.rb` lacks the batches tables and column.
- `config/database.mysql.yml`, `config/database.sqlite.yml` and `saas/config/database.yml` all point the `queue` database at `migrations_paths: db/queue_migrate`, which does not exist in the repo. Fresh installs load `db/queue_schema.rb`; existing databases (SaaS production, self-hosters) need a migration file in that directory.
- Fizzy does not call `SolidQueue::Batch` anywhere. `config/recurring.yml` lines 19 and 50 call `SolidQueue::Job.clear_finished_in_batches`, which still exists at v1.7.0 (`app/models/solid_queue/job/clearable.rb:13`); the new `SolidQueue::Batch.clear_finished_in_batches` is a separate, additional method.
- The UUID primary-key shims (`config/initializers/uuid_primary_keys.rb`, `uuid_framework_models.rb`) only fire for `binary(16)`/`blob(16)`/`uuid` columns; the batches migration uses `bigint`, matching every other solid_queue table.

**Mitigation:**

1. Run `bin/rails solid_queue:update` (the generator defaults to `--database queue`, so it writes into `db/queue_migrate/`). Commit the generated `*_add_batches_to_solid_queue.rb`; it uses `if_not_exists: true` throughout, so it is safe on fresh installs that already loaded the new schema.
2. Run `bin/rails db:migrate` and regenerate `db/queue_schema.rb` (`bin/rails db:schema:dump`), or hand-add the two tables and the `batch_id` column + index to match the generator template at `lib/generators/solid_queue/install/templates/db/queue_schema.rb`. Diff the result against that template.
3. Deploy the migration with or after the gem bump. Ordering is not critical: old code ignores the extra column, new code tolerates its absence. Until it runs, each dispatcher logs one `SolidQueue.deprecator` warning at boot.
4. Optional: add a recurring task `clear_solid_queue_finished_batches` with `command: "SolidQueue::Batch.clear_finished_in_batches(sleep_between_batches: 0.3)"` alongside the existing job clearers, so finished batch rows are pruned once batches are in use. Not needed while nothing enqueues batches.
